title: Substitution systems with deletion need three or more colors for complexity

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Substitution systems with deletion need three or more colors for complexity

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Among two-color substitution systems that allow elements to be destroyed, those with slow growth produce only simple repetitive patterns, but allowing three or four colors immediately makes patterns as random-looking as those of cellular automata possible.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: allowing elements to have three or four colors rather than just two immediately makes much more complicated behavior possible.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 3, “The World of Simple Programs”; section “Substitution Systems” (from p. 82), p. 86. Scope: neighbor-dependent substitution systems with creation and destruction of elements

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch03-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existence of complex three- or four-color examples is directly computable. The universal simplicity assertion for two-color systems is only fully decidable after tightly bounding the rule grammar and ultimate-behavior criterion.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate bounded two-, three-, and four-color deletion-capable substitution rule spaces under the book's growth constraint, then measure periodicity and random-like statistics. A complex slow-growing two-color counterexample refutes the first part, while verified three-color examples confirm possibility.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The full rule space depends on maximum replacement length and neighborhood.

Slow growth and random-looking require thresholds.

Finite runs may miss long transients.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.7
data existence: 0.9
discriminating power: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The existence of complicated three- and four-color examples is a finite check of published rules. The claim that every slow-growth two-color deleting substitution is merely repetitive ranges over an open-ended format and, in the source, rests on observation of the rules that were tried. Short rules can be re-enumerated now; the unrestricted two-color statement cannot be closed by that enumeration.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Resimulate the published three- and four-color slow-growth substitution systems and test them for randomness-like statistics; that checks the existence half. For two colors, either prove that every slow-growth deleting rule is eventually periodic or exhaust a declared finite subclass. An incompressible two-color slow-growth example refutes the restrictive half.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The source presents the two-color statement as what the search found, which is weaker than a proof.

Block length is unbounded, so the two-color family is infinite and a search of short rules does not cover it.

Slow growth and simple repetitive pattern need numeric definitions.
